analysis:
The only change is a documentation addition in docs/architecture/inference.md (head lines 790-806, near the base request flow diagram). It describes a new per-prefix-cache-scope prompt token cache (PromptTokenCache) in LocalTokenizerBridge, linear-time ChatTemplateLoopRewrites for Gemma 4 and GPT-OSS templates, and a DARKBLOOM_TTFT_PROMPT_CACHE=0 kill switch. No code is in the supplied evidence, so no concrete regression can be cited. The base units supplied (lines 1236-1777) are unchanged context and were read only for orientation.

Security-relevant questions for later review once the implementation is visible:
- The cache holds prompt-derived token IDs in memory, which relates to A-001, T-028 and T-041. The doc states that reuse never crosses a cache scope, so the scope must be the coordinator-authored cacheSalt and must not be caller-controlled.
- Piece-level token reuse could create a timing or TTFT oracle. Within one scope this is the same narrower same-account channel already accepted as SEC-035.
- Retention and eviction bounds of the cache are not described. Unbounded growth would be an availability concern (T-016 and T-029 class), and entries should be purged on KEK wipe, unload or process exit.
- The four-core parallel encode for long prompts could affect availability and fairness against other requests.
- The doc says the cache does not write to disk. The implementation should be confirmed not to persist token IDs, since that would create an at-rest artifact outside the SSD tier's HMAC and KEK posture.
- Sampled background comparisons use the served template, so it must be confirmed that they do not log prompt content.
- The template rewrites (ChatTemplateLoopRewrites) change how prompts are rendered, so equivalence with the original template, including tool and system roles, matters for prompt-injection and role-confusion boundaries.

None of these can be verified from the documentation alone. The documented design includes mitigations: a scope boundary, equality checks and a kill switch.
